title: A Practical Guide to Comparing Similar Websites
content:
Compare two websites by trying to complete the same task on both. “Find a downloadable invoice without contacting support” produces more useful evidence than “Which homepage looks better?” The first question reveals navigation, account requirements, terminology, accessibility, and recovery behavior. The second mostly reveals personal taste.

This guide describes an editorial comparison method you can adapt to directories, software services, research portals, or shops. It is not a formal usability study. The aim is to make a decision traceable: another person should understand what you tried, what you observed, and why those observations matter to your situation.

Choose a task before opening tabs

Write a one-sentence scenario naming the user, goal, and constraint. For example, a volunteer needs a public dataset in a reusable format without creating an account. Choose candidates that plausibly satisfy that scenario. Comparing an enterprise analytics platform with a public chart gallery is only useful if you acknowledge that they serve different jobs.

Keep the starting conditions comparable. Use the same device class, similar connection conditions, and the same account state where possible. Record when one site requires a paid plan or an invitation. Do not silently compare a logged-in premium view on one website with a public landing page on another.

Make a short observation sheet before browsing. Useful columns include task outcome, steps taken, blocked actions, evidence URL, plan limitation, and date checked. Separate a directly observed result from a promise in marketing copy. “The pricing page lists CSV export” and “a sample export opened correctly” are different levels of evidence.

Compare essential constraints before preferences

Identify disqualifying requirements: an accessible keyboard path, a particular export format, a region restriction, or an account policy your organization cannot accept. A weighted score should not hide failure on a mandatory requirement. Mark that candidate unsuitable for this task even if its visual design is excellent.

For accessibility, use the W3C WAI preliminary checks as a starting point. They cover examples such as headings, keyboard access, and form labels, while explicitly warning that easy checks are not a comprehensive assessment. Report the specific barrier you encountered rather than declaring a whole website compliant or noncompliant from a brief visit.

For performance, distinguish what happened on your device from a population-level conclusion. Google's Web Vitals guidance separates loading, responsiveness, and visual stability. Those dimensions provide useful vocabulary. A single quick page load is not evidence that all visitors experience the site the same way, particularly across accounts, regions, devices, and network conditions.

A hypothetical dataset comparison

Imagine comparing three public data websites for a student project. This hypothetical exercise needs a monthly table, source attribution, and a downloadable file. Candidate A has attractive charts but no visible export on the public page. Candidate B exposes a CSV file and a methodology note. Candidate C provides a download only after registration.

The evaluator does not claim B has better data simply because downloading is easier. They inspect the table period, column definitions, and update note. A downloadable file can still contain unsuitable measurements. They also check whether C's account condition is acceptable for the assignment instead of treating registration as inherently bad.

The resulting note says B is provisionally suitable for the current project because the public table and documentation meet the stated needs. A remains unverified for export. C remains an alternative if registration is permitted. These are local conclusions based on a specific task, not a league table of overall website quality.

Use scores only after writing the evidence

If a numerical comparison helps, define each score in observable terms. A three-point export scale might distinguish unavailable, available with manual cleanup, and usable in the required format. Avoid assigning arbitrary decimals that suggest precision the review does not have. Explain any weighting before seeing which candidate it favors.

Keep cost comparisons explicit about the unit. A monthly subscription, per-seat charge, usage allowance, and annual commitment are different obligations. Check the current official plan page when cost is part of the decision. If you cannot confirm an important fee or limit, leave it unknown rather than converting a vague sales claim into a price.

Ask a second person to repeat the most important task if the choice will affect a team. A fresh attempt can reveal terminology assumptions you have stopped noticing. It still does not create a statistically representative study. Treat the repetition as a practical cross-check, and preserve disagreements rather than averaging them into a misleadingly tidy verdict.

Checklist for a decision somebody can revisit

  • Name the exact task and intended user.
  • List requirements that cannot be traded away.
  • Record device, account state, and date.
  • Try the complete task rather than only the homepage.
  • Capture evidence without exposing personal account information.
  • Separate direct observations from advertised capabilities.
  • Describe accessibility barriers precisely.
  • Label unknown costs, permissions, and export limits.
  • Explain why the chosen trade-offs fit this situation.
  • Set a review trigger when plans or requirements change.

Keep the final recommendation short enough to use. A clear sentence stating the selected candidate, the decisive evidence, and one unresolved limitation is more actionable than a decorative comparison chart with no decision. Store the observation sheet beside it so the next reviewer can inspect the reasoning.
excerpt: Compare similar websites with a shared task, observable evidence, accessibility checks, and explicit trade-offs instead of a misleading overall score.
